lesson.title: The Closed Interval Method: A Four-Step Recipe for Absolute Extrema
lesson.summary: The Closed Interval Method packages the Candidates Test into an explicit four-step algorithm: confirm continuity, find the critical numbers inside the interval, evaluate the function at those critical numbers and at both endpoints, then compare to read off the absolute maximum and minimum.
lesson.body:
Given a function f continuous on a closed interval [a, b], the Closed Interval Method is simply the Candidates Test written out as an explicit procedure. Step one: confirm f is continuous on [a, b], so the Extreme Value Theorem applies and an absolute max and min are guaranteed to exist. Step two: find f'(x), then solve f'(x) = 0 or locate where f' is undefined, keeping only the critical numbers that fall strictly inside (a, b). Step three: evaluate f at every critical number found in step two, and separately evaluate f at the two endpoints a and b. Step four: compare all of those output values, the largest one is the absolute maximum of f on [a, b], and the smallest one is the absolute minimum, each attained at whichever input value or values produced it.

Apply this to f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 1 on the closed interval [-2, 2]. Step one, f is a polynomial, so it is continuous everywhere, including on [-2, 2]. Step two, f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 3(x^2 - 1) = 3(x - 1)(x + 1), so f'(x) = 0 at x = -1 and x = 1, and both lie strictly inside (-2, 2), so both qualify as candidates. Step three, evaluate f at the two critical numbers and the two endpoints: f(-2) = (-8) - 3(-2) + 1 = -8 + 6 + 1 = -1. f(-1) = (-1) - 3(-1) + 1 = -1 + 3 + 1 = 3. f(1) = 1 - 3 + 1 = -1. f(2) = 8 - 6 + 1 = 3.

Step four, compare the four values: -1, 3, -1, 3. The largest value is 3, attained at both x = -1 and x = 2, so the absolute maximum of f on [-2, 2] is 3. The smallest value is -1, attained at both x = -2 and x = 1, so the absolute minimum is -1. Every candidate got evaluated, nothing was skipped, and the comparison in step four is what finally separates the winners from the rest. This is the payoff of the whole chapter sequence: monotonicity and the sign chart of f' locate local behavior, concavity and the second derivative describe how the graph bends, and the Closed Interval Method uses all of that groundwork, plus a direct comparison of finitely many numbers, to pin down the absolute largest and smallest values a function reaches on a closed interval, no guessing required.
